headline: Tabcorp's acquisition of Bet Makers is a strategic pivot toward B2B technology and global tote distribution rather than a pure earnings play
reasoning: Tom Waterhouse views Tabcorp's acquisition of Bet Makers as a strategic technology purchase rather than an earnings-driven deal. The value in the wagering industry has shifted from consumer-facing brands to suppliers, and Tabcorp is buying the pipes — the technology, global distribution, and global tote service. Bet Makers also manages trading and platform services for around 40 bookmakers, giving Tabcorp a B2B services revenue stream. Tabcorp's existing assets — vision rights, data, and its tote business — can now be packaged into a global product. The move is seen as necessary given increasing taxation, regulation, and advertising restrictions squeezing Australian B2C wagering businesses.
quote: Look we've been focused for the last seven years with Waterhouse VC on the size of the industry. So we were a shareholder of Bet makers, really liked the business because it was a key supplier to the racing industry. And I think what Tabcorp have done with that acquisition is not necessarily buying for the earnings. It's really buying the pipes, they're buying the technology, they're buying the global distribution, they're buying the global tote service they've got. And if they can integrate that in technology with all the assets they have, well then they have a very different business. So the value in the industry is really shifted from the consumer facing businesses. So like all the household names that you know, to really the suppliers in the industry. And I think it's a very strategic move and a very interesting acquisition for Tabcorp.

headline: Avoiding B2C betting operators, focusing on infrastructure/supply-side winners in US prediction market boom
reasoning: Tom Waterhouse notes that US prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi have a significant regulatory advantage over traditional sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings — they can operate in states where online sports betting is not legalised and avoid state gambling taxes. Waterhouse VC does not invest in B2C operators (Tabcorp, Sportsbet, FanDuel, DraftKings) but is focused on identifying which suppliers or infrastructure providers will win as prediction markets scale. The key structural challenge is liquidity: unlike a bookmaker that takes the other side, prediction market exchanges require a market maker to hold escrow for full potential payouts, creating enormous liquidity demands. Waterhouse draws an analogy to Betfair's Australian launch ~20 years ago, suggesting the 'pipes' — liquidity providers and infrastructure — are where the real opportunity lies. The open question is whether large financial institutions, incumbent bookmakers, or professional betting syndicates will emerge as the dominant market makers.
quote: For us, we're not sure. We don't invest in these B2C. We don't invest in a Tabcorp or a Sportsbet or a FanDuel or DraftKings. But for us, it's really interesting what types or what suppliers can win in this space. And a little bit like what happened with Betfair when it came launched here about 20 years ago. The area that we think is really interesting is unlike a bookmaker that puts up the odds and takes the bets. If you're a prediction market, they're the other side of the ledger has to be put up by somebody. And so it's not because they're not a bookmaker, they're an exchange. And so for us, who is going to win that market, make a race. Is it going to be the large financial institutions? Is it going to be the other bookmakers like a FanDuel or DraftKings, or is it going to be the professional betting groups?
episode_title: Tom's betting on the pipe stocks

headline: Flutter's share price has declined sharply as prediction markets and new entrants challenge the assumed dominance of scale operators like FanDuel
reasoning: Tom Waterhouse notes that the conventional investment thesis in US online wagering was that scale operators — FanDuel (owned by Flutter) and DraftKings — would win due to their state licenses, marketing budgets, and flywheel advantages. However, prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket can operate in states where FanDuel and DraftKings cannot and are exempt from state gambling taxes because their products are classified as federally regulated financial instruments. This has upended the certainty around who the long-term winners in the US market will be.
quote: And really, if you were an investor in the space, you were betting that scale wins. Those large operators had those state licenses, could use the massive balance sheet to spend a lot of money on marketing, acquire customers better experience. We've talked about it before, the flywheel effect. And so you really went, okay, well, FanDuel has the scale, DraftKings has the scale. They can pay the taxes, get the state licenses. What's happened now in the last six months, especially now that you can offer these prediction markets, can offer Maltese, which is the highest margin product for the bookmakers on sports betting, is that they've got this regulatory ability to take bets in states that DraftKings and FanDuel cannot. So they can take bets in California and Texas, but they also don't have to pay the state gambling taxes because they're a federally regulated financial product.
